title: ITER: the parts of the machine
drawing_note: Original cross-section drawn by the course from ITER's published dimensions (plasma radius, vessel and cryostat size, coil counts). It is approximately to scale; coil positions and shapes are simplified, and the ports, which pass between the toroidal field coils, are drawn in the same plane as the coils.

parts.name: Plasma
parts.does: The fuel: a mixture of deuterium and tritium, heated to about 150 million °C. The magnetic field holds the plasma ring away from the walls, and fusion happens here.
parts.number: Major radius $R = 6.2\ \text{m}$, plasma volume $V \approx 830\ \text{m}^3$, planned fusion power $P_\text{fusion} = 500\ \text{MW}$
parts.number_note: ITER's facts page gives $830\ \text{m}^3$; some of its machine pages give $840\ \text{m}^3$.
parts.hard: The plasma must be hot, dense and well confined at the same time. It is unstable in many ways, and all the heat that leaves it must be taken away by the divertor and the wall.
parts.find: the hot, ionised fuel, held by the magnetic field in the middle of the vessel
parts.hint: It is not a solid part: it fills the D-shaped space inside the vessel.

parts.name: Blanket modules and first wall
parts.does: 440 modules cover the inner walls of the vacuum vessel. Their first wall faces the plasma. The blanket takes the heat and the fast neutrons and shields the vessel and the magnets. Later in ITER's life some modules will be replaced by test blanket modules that try out ways to breed tritium from lithium.
parts.number: $440$ modules, each about $1\ \text{m} \cdot 1.5\ \text{m}$ and up to $4.6\ \text{t}$; cooling water removes up to $736\ \text{MW}$ of heat
parts.hard: The first wall is hit by heat, particles and neutrons. In 2023 ITER decided to change the first-wall armour from beryllium to tungsten. The modules must be aligned to about $10\ \text{mm}$ and changed by remote handling.
parts.find: the lining of modules that faces the plasma all around the inside of the vessel
parts.hint: Look just outside the plasma, but not at the bottom.

parts.name: Divertor
parts.does: The exhaust system at the bottom of the vessel. Field lines at the edge of the plasma lead the heat, the helium ash and other impurities onto its targets.
parts.number: $54$ cassettes of $10\ \text{t}$; heat load on the targets about $10\ \text{MW}/\text{m}^2$ (steady) and $20\ \text{MW}/\text{m}^2$ (slow transients)
parts.hard: The highest surface heat loads in the machine, about ten times those on a spacecraft entering the atmosphere. The targets are armoured with tungsten, the metal with the highest melting point, and cooled with water. The cassettes are changed by remote handling.
parts.find: the exhaust at the bottom of the vessel that takes the heat and the helium ash
parts.hint: Follow the edge of the plasma down to where its legs touch the wall.

parts.name: Vacuum vessel
parts.does: A sealed, double-walled stainless steel container around the plasma. It keeps the vacuum, holds the blanket and the divertor, and is the first safety barrier. Cooling water flows between its two walls, and steel blocks there add shielding.
parts.number: Outer diameter $19.4\ \text{m}$, height $11.4\ \text{m}$, mass about $5200\ \text{t}$ (about $8500\ \text{t}$ with the blanket and the divertor)
parts.hard: It is welded together from huge sections with very small tolerances. It has 44 openings (ports), must stay leak-tight and must withstand large electromagnetic forces.
parts.find: the double-walled steel container that holds the vacuum around the plasma
parts.hint: It is the D-shaped double wall just outside the blanket.

parts.name: Toroidal field coils
parts.does: 18 D-shaped superconducting coils around the vessel. They make the toroidal magnetic field that goes around the ring.
parts.number: $18$ coils of $\text{Nb}_3\text{Sn}$, peak field $11.8\ \text{T}$, about $330\ \text{t}$ each, stored energy $41\ \text{GJ}$
parts.hard: They are superconducting only when cooled to about $4\ \text{K}$ ($-269\ ^\circ\text{C}$) with supercritical helium, right next to a $150$-million-degree plasma. The magnetic forces on them are enormous.
parts.find: the big D-shaped coils that make the magnetic field going around the ring
parts.hint: They are D-shaped and surround the vessel; there are 18 of them.

parts.name: Poloidal field coils
parts.does: Six ring-shaped coils outside the toroidal field coils. Their field shapes the plasma, holds it in position and helps to keep it stable.
parts.number: $6$ coils of $\text{NbTi}$, peak field $6\ \text{T}$, the heaviest $400\ \text{t}$
parts.hard: The two largest are so wide that they set the size of the cryostat (inner diameter $28\ \text{m}$). Their currents must be controlled all the time to keep the plasma in place.
parts.find: the six horizontal rings that shape the plasma and hold it in position
parts.hint: In a cross-section each ring is a small rectangle outside the D-shaped coils.

parts.name: Central solenoid
parts.does: A tall stack of six coil modules in the middle of the machine. Like the primary winding of a transformer, a changing current in it induces the large current in the plasma ring.
parts.number: $6$ modules of $\text{Nb}_3\text{Sn}$, $13\ \text{m}$ tall, $1000\ \text{t}$, peak field $13\ \text{T}$, stored energy $6.4\ \text{GJ}$
parts.hard: Its current must change quickly, again and again, so the coil is pushed and pulled by large, repeating forces. Inductive drive alone also limits how long a pulse can last.
parts.find: the tall stack of coils in the middle that induces the plasma current, like a transformer
parts.hint: Look at the centre of the machine, next to the axis.

parts.name: Thermal shield
parts.does: Stainless steel panels between the very cold magnets and the warm parts: one layer between the vacuum vessel and the magnets, one inside the cryostat wall. Cooled by helium, they stop heat radiation from reaching the magnets.
parts.number: About $5000\ \text{m}^2$ of panels, cooled to $80\ \text{K}$ to $100\ \text{K}$, up to $25\ \text{m}$ tall
parts.hard: Large, thin panels must fit into narrow gaps between the vessel, the coils and the cryostat without touching them.
parts.find: the cooled panels that stop heat radiation reaching the cold magnets
parts.hint: Thin layers: one just outside the vacuum vessel, one just inside the cryostat wall.

parts.name: Cryostat
parts.does: A huge stainless steel vacuum chamber around the whole tokamak. The vacuum inside it insulates the very cold magnets from the warm building.
parts.number: Volume $16000\ \text{m}^3$, inner diameter $28\ \text{m}$, almost $30\ \text{m}$ tall, mass $3850\ \text{t}$
parts.hard: The largest stainless steel high-vacuum chamber ever built. Its base alone ($1250\ \text{t}$) was the heaviest single load in assembly, and it has over 200 penetrations that must all be vacuum-tight.
parts.find: the giant vacuum chamber that surrounds the whole machine
parts.hint: It is the outermost wall in the drawing.

parts.name: Ports
parts.does: Openings in the vacuum vessel at the top, at the middle and at the bottom. Through them go the heating systems, the diagnostics, fuelling, vacuum pumping and the remote-handling tools.
parts.hard: Every opening is a gap in the shielding that must be filled and sealed. The ports pass between the toroidal field coils and through the cryostat, so all parts must fit very precisely.
parts.find: the openings at the top, middle and bottom of the vessel that lead out through the cryostat
parts.hint: Look for the ducts that lead from the vessel out through the cryostat wall.

parts.name: Heating systems
parts.does: They heat the plasma from outside. Neutral beam injection fires beams of fast neutral deuterium atoms into the plasma; ion cyclotron heating (radio waves) and electron cyclotron heating (microwaves) give energy to the ions and to the electrons. Beams and waves can also push the plasma current.
parts.number: Planned $P_\text{heating} = 50\ \text{MW}$ for $Q = 10$. Beams: $2 \cdot 16.5\ \text{MW}$ at $1\ \text{MeV}$; electron cyclotron: $170\ \text{GHz}$, $40\ \text{MW}$ at first (later up to $67\ \text{MW}$); ion cyclotron: $40\ \text{MHz}$ to $55\ \text{MHz}$, $10\ \text{MW}$ at first (later $20\ \text{MW}$)
parts.hard: Ions must be accelerated to $1\ \text{MeV}$ and neutralised; the microwaves come from about 1-MW gyrotrons. All this power must reach the plasma through ports in a radiation environment.
parts.find: the systems that heat the plasma from outside with beams and waves
parts.hint: In the drawing they sit in the ports on the right.

parts.name: Diagnostics
parts.does: Instruments that measure the plasma: its temperature and density, its shape and position, the radiation and the neutrons that show the fusion power. The measurements are used to control the plasma and for research.
parts.hard: They must work next to the plasma, in strong neutron and heat loads, and look at it through narrow openings in the shielding. Most sit in port plugs.
parts.find: the instruments that measure the plasma, mostly in port plugs
parts.hint: In the drawing they are in the ports on the left; dashed lines show their lines of sight.

parts.name: Cryopumps
parts.does: Pumps that catch gas on very cold panels coated with activated charcoal and cooled with supercritical helium. They pump the helium ash and the unburnt fuel out of the vessel and keep the vacuum in the cryostat.
parts.number: $6$ torus exhaust pumps, $2$ cryostat cryopumps, $4$ for the neutral beam injectors
parts.hard: Helium is hard to catch. The charcoal (made from coconut shells) traps it only when it is extremely cold, and the panels fill up, so they must be emptied regularly by warming them.
parts.find: the pumps with very cold panels that take the helium ash and unburnt fuel out of the vessel
parts.hint: In the drawing one sits in a lower port, below the level of the divertor.

points: $Q$ compares the fusion power made in the plasma with the heating power put into the plasma.
$Q = 1$ is **scientific breakeven**: the plasma makes as much fusion power as it receives.
ITER's goal is $Q = 10$: $500\ \text{MW}$ of fusion power from $50\ \text{MW}$ of heating, in pulses of $400\ \text{s}$ to $600\ \text{s}$.

$Q$ is a plasma gain, **not electricity**. ITER will not turn its heat into electricity, and the whole plant needs far more electrical power than the $50\ \text{MW}$ that reaches the plasma (over $300\ \text{MW}$, according to Wikipedia).

schedule.baseline: The baseline that ITER presented on 3 July 2024 (it replaced the earlier baseline).

items.event: The ITER Members choose the site in southern France (June 2005).
Start of Research Operation (SRO): the first plasma experiments with the full machine.

members.share_note: Shares of the construction costs. As host, the European Union pays the largest part.

cooperation.name: Kazakhstan
cooperation.note: through the National Nuclear Center; extended in 2025

site.text: Saint-Paul-lez-Durance in southern France, next to the CEA Cadarache research centre. The 180-hectare site has a 42-hectare platform in the middle where the machine is built.
